title: Reading engine-bearing wear
introduction:
A bearing's worn surface is a little witness statement from inside the engine. I compare the location and shape of its marks with the drawing before interpreting them: scattered pits, broad scratches and wear confined to an edge tell different stories.

Read the illustrated examples from left to right across each row and match them to the corresponding entries below. This is a visual recognition guide for exposed bearing shells. It pairs each pattern with the stated failure condition; it does not provide bearing access, clearance limits, journal measurements or a replacement procedure. Oil level, oil pressure and bearing clearance answer different questions, so this picture cannot stand in for those checks.

items.name: Use an already exposed bearing
items.detail: This reference begins with a bearing surface available for visual comparison. Obtain the engine-specific access and reassembly procedure before dismantling anything; this illustration is not an engine teardown sequence.

items.name: Protect yourself while handling parts
items.detail: Wear eye and ear protection when servicing a vehicle, and protective gloves when handling components with pointed or sharp edges. Failure to follow these precautions can cause serious personal injury.

items.name: If inspection involves work around the vehicle
items.detail: disable remote start, if equipped, through the Central Display under Vehicle settings > Remote Start Setup before vehicle service or inspection. Unexpected remote starting can cause personal injury or death. Switch the ignition OFF and remove the key from the vehicle to prevent another person accidentally starting the engine, which can cause serious personal injury. These vehicle-start precautions apply to work around the car; comparing an already removed shell at a bench does not itself require vehicle access.

edits.why: The entries identify pictured conditions and their stated meanings; they are comparison labels, not a sequence of repair operations.

edits.text: Look for cratering—pits in the bearing surface. This pattern indicates fatigue failure.
edits.why: The matching drawing shows scattered surface cavities. I distinguish those pits from the elongated marks in the scratching example before assigning the fatigue label.

edits.text: Look for spot glazing—localized glazed patches on the bearing surface. This pattern indicates incorrect seating.
edits.why: The useful distinction is the localized glazing rather than a field of pits or scratches. The guide associates that appearance with how the bearing was seated; it does not identify the particular seating error.

edits.text: Look for scratching across the bearing surface. This pattern indicates dirty engine oil.
edits.why: Compare the drawn scratch marks with the pitted fatigue example. This association directs attention to oil contamination without identifying where the contamination originated.

edits.text: Look for exposed base material where the bearing surface has worn through. This pattern indicates poor lubrication.
edits.why: The distinction is loss of the working surface, rather than marks confined to it. The illustration associates that damage with poor lubrication but does not establish its underlying cause or an oil-pressure value.

edits.text: Look for wear along both edges of the bearing. This pattern indicates a damaged journal.
edits.why: Wear location matters here. The journal is the shaft surface that runs against the bearing; the guide connects damage there with wear at both bearing edges.

edits.text: Look for wear along one edge of the bearing. This pattern indicates either a tapered journal or a bearing that is not seated.
edits.why: Keep both possibilities open. I use the edge pattern to identify the stated alternatives, not to choose between them: the drawing supplies no measurement or seating check that resolves that branch.
